rich_summary: This passage recounts the miraculous revival of Abhimanyu’s stillborn son. Uttara, overwhelmed with grief, laments over the lifeless child while the royal women gather around her. Krishna, moved by her sorrow, withdraws the destructive Brahma-weapon and vows—by the truthfulness of his life, his devotion to righteousness, and his victories over evil—that the child will live. His words manifest power: the infant stirs and returns to life, bringing immense relief and celebration to the Kuru household. The child is later named Parikshit because he is born when the Kuru line is nearly extinguished after the great war. The episode underscores Krishna’s divine authority, the sanctity of truth, and the fragile survival of the Kuru dynasty through this single heir.

highlight_spans.why: Uttara’s grief-stricken lament sets the emotional tone, showing the devastation after the war and the fragility of the last heir.
The imagery of the grieving princess compared to a deer pierced by a hunter captures the vulnerability of the surviving royal family.
Krishna withdraws the Brahma-weapon and promises to restore the child’s life—this marks the turning point of the episode.
Krishna invokes the truth of his life and deeds as a sacred vow, demonstrating the epic’s belief in truth as a cosmic power.
The moment the child becomes animate signifies the preservation of the Kuru lineage and the hope that follows devastation.

top_scenes.scene_text: Krishna standing beside the grieving Uttara in the dim birth chamber, raising his hand in solemn vow as the lifeless infant lies before them and the royal women watch in despair.
The miraculous instant when the newborn Parikshit begins to move while a radiant glow fills the chamber and the women of the Kuru household look on in astonished joy.
A celebratory scene in Hastinapura with decorated streets, banners flying, dancers and singers performing as news spreads that the Kuru heir has been saved.
